allegations

/al-uh-GAY-shunz/ — 'AL-uh-GAY-shuns' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Allegations is claims that someone has done something wrong, made without proof yet.

The mayor denied the allegations that she had misused campaign funds.

Example

An anonymous letter made allegations that the company was dumping chemicals into the river. No court had found them true, no inspector had confirmed them, but reporters printed the claims and demanded answers.

Allegations are accusations of wrongdoing that haven't yet been proven. Once a court confirms wrongdoing, it becomes a 'finding' or a 'conviction'; before that, it stays merely an allegation.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

accusations: Accusations are claims that someone has done something wrong. An accusation can be flung in a hallway argument and proven or dropped a day later; allegations carry an extra signal — the claim is specific, often made in print or to authorities, and nothing about it has been proven yet.

claims: Claims are statements asserted as true, without proof yet, and they can be about anything at all — a product's mileage, a neighbor's fence line. Allegations are a narrower kind of claim: they always accuse someone of wrongdoing, and choosing the word deliberately signals that nothing has been proven.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

proof: evidence that establishes something is true

confirmation: an official statement that something is verified

Where it sits · how official the accusation is

rumor → allegations → indictment

rumor vs. allegations: Rumor is weaker than allegation — a rumor spreads informally with no clear source, while an allegation is a specific claim often made to authorities or in print.

indictment vs. allegations: Indictment is stronger than allegation — an allegation is just an unproven claim, but an indictment is a formal legal charge backed by some evidence.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — al- (ad-): to, toward (Latin)

root — leg-: to bring forward, to assert (Latin)

suffix — -ation: act or result of (Latin)

Put it together: Latin allegare meant 'to bring forward as evidence or an excuse.' An allegation is what someone brings forward and asserts — before anyone has proven it true.

Use the root in a new word: delegate: With the deadline looming, the manager finally learned to delegate.

Word Choice

Very common in news and legal writing; using 'allegations' instead of 'crimes' is a deliberate signal that nothing has been proven yet.
